title: Control plane decomposition & regional routing playbook
body:
Purpose:
This is a working playbook sketch to clarify service boundaries for the control plane components we own, and to capture a regional routing decision model people can copy into RFCs and runbooks. Focus: API gateway responsibilities, orchestration (control-plane core), runtime adapters (GPU/CPU pools), and how ownership shifts when we run multi-region.

High-level service decomposition (intended):
- API gateway (edge team): ingress, auth, tenant scoping, initial request validation, short-circuiting (rate limits, quota), and primary routing hints (region preference, model / variant selector). Not responsible for model compatibility checks beyond surface level (e.g., model id exists).
- Orchestration / Control-plane core (platform-engineering): policy evaluation, placement decision, global state (capacity map), rollout policies, deployment metadata, canary logic, route fallbacks and A/B selection. Exposes policy API consumed by gateway and autoscaler.
- Runtime adapters (serving-runtime interface): translate placement decisions into concrete fleet operations (allocate GPU slot, pin model binary, configure quantization profile). Responsible for per-cluster capacity accounting and local health signals.
- SRE / Observability: owns incident runbooks, cross-region outage detection, and the tracing/metric dashboards; collaborates on SLA targets for each component.

Routing decision model (step-by-step):
1) Gateway receives request -> extracts tenant & model intent + optional region hint. Apply auth & quota.
2) Gateway requests placement from orchestration service with (tenant, model, region_hint, latency_slo, cost_tier).
3) Orchestration evaluates:
   - Preferred region availability (capacity map)
   - Latency SLO vs estimated p99 for candidate clusters
   - Cost tier (e.g., on-demand vs reserved)
   - Canary/rollout policy binding for tenant/model
   - Model compatibility (via model metadata cached from model catalog service)
   - Fallback rules (force cross-region if no compatible capacity)
4) Orchestration returns route: {target_cluster, adapter_endpoint, expected_latency_ms, fallback_list}.
5) Gateway forwards request to runtime adapter endpoint. If adapter rejects (capacity/health), gateway retries orchestration for next fallback.

Region-aware ownership rules (practical callouts):
- Gateway must be region-aware but stateless in terms of global policy (does not hold authoritative capacity map).
- Orchestration is authoritative for capacity/rollout but must tolerate eventual consistency; ownership includes sharding logic for regional caches and a single leader for write operations (per-region leader + global coordinator).
- Runtime adapters own local health + exact placement operations; they must expose a stable contract (health, tokenized lease, eviction reasons).

Failure scenarios & responsibilities (who acts first):
- Regional control-plane control-loss (leader unresponsive): orchestration should promote standby leader; gateway should consult regional fallback list and route to next region. SRE triggers incident and capacity borrowing.
- Adapter-level eviction (OOM / model crash): adapter emits structured event -> orchestration marks slot unhealthy and triggers reschedule; gateway retries with adapter-suggested fallback.
- Model rollout causing regression across region: orchestration can globally pause rollout and trigger global rollback; rollback owner: product + platform-engineering to coordinate.

Operational boundaries (TL;DR ownership matrix):
- Auth & quotas: API gateway (policy enforcement), but quota counters replicated to orchestration for global quotas.
- Routing decision (final): Orchestration returns canonical route; gateway executes.
- Telemetry ownership: adapters emit raw metrics; orchestration normalizes and tags; observability owns storage/alerts.

Design constraints & rationale (why split this way):
- Keep gateway lightweight & horizontally scalable; avoid embedding long-running policy logic to minimize cold-start surface.
- Centralize policy in orchestration so we can evolve rollout semantics without changing gateway code across many languages.
- Let adapters be the narrow hardware-specific translation layer so new hardware types (e.g., future accelerators) only need adapter changes.

Practical runbook snippets (to copy into ops docs):
- "If region X reports >30% slot error rate for >5m, mark as degraded, remove from primary routing, and notify SRE. Orchestration will drain canary traffic automatically"
- "When promoting regional leader: validate global state snapshot is less than 2m behind; otherwise run snapshot catchup job."

Open questions / TODOs (working list):
- How much policy should live in gateway for fast failover vs. central orchestration latency? (tradeoff: fail-fast vs single source of truth)
- Exact schema for orchestration's fallback_list (should include cost delta and estimated added latency).
- Lease TTL semantics between orchestration and adapters (currently prototyped in PLAT-4121).
- Cross-region data compliance hooks: add a flag in routing response that the gateway logs for audit (GDPR/Paid-region tenants).

Action items (next 3 sprints):
- Sprint A: finalize fallback_list schema + update gateway client (Ethan).
- Sprint B: implement adapter lease TTL enforcement and eviction reason codes (Raj).
- Sprint C: run chaos experiment that kills regional leader and validate fallback behavior (SRE + Platform).

Notes to reviewers:
- This doc is intentionally informal; please annotate sections you want formalized into an RFC. Link any relevant Jira tickets into the TODOs above.

Slack refs / historical context:
- See slack thread: #platform-arch "regional routing sketch" (Nov 2025) for early whiteboard screenshots.
- Prototype work lives in repo: control-plane/placement-v2 (PR linked above).

End.
